changes.before: Create a view customer_orders with customer_id, name, total_orders, paid_orders and paid_cents. Include every customer, even those without orders. Count all their orders, count only status="paid" orders, and sum only paid amounts. Missing totals must be zero. Amounts are nonnegative integer cents.
changes.after: Count all orders and paid orders without losing customers who have none.

before: A dashboard may need several summaries from the same data. Aggregation combines rows, using functions such as COUNT and SUM. Conditional aggregation adds a decision inside the aggregate so different summary columns can include different rows. Here, a customer can have paid, pending or cancelled orders.

Start from customers and LEFT JOIN orders using the customer ID. A left join keeps a customer even when no order matches. The unmatched order columns become NULL. COUNT(*) would count that retained row as one, so use COUNT(o.id) to count only real orders; COUNT(column) skips NULL.

CASE turns a condition into a value before SUM adds it.
```sql
WITH orders(status, cents) AS (VALUES ('paid', 300), ('pending', 500), ('paid', 200))
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM orders;
```
This returns 2 paid orders and 500 paid cents. The pending amount is deliberately excluded.

GROUP BY chooses which rows belong to each summary. Group by customer ID and name. Names alone are unsafe because two different customers can share a name. Aliases such as c for customers and o for orders shorten qualified column names, including c.id and o.customer_id.

This example keeps a customer with no order.
```sql
WITH customers(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2)),
orders(id, customer_id) AS (VALUES (10, 1))
SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders
FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY c.id;
```
Customer 1 has one order; customer 2 has zero. An inner join would lose customer 2 entirely.

Do not place WHERE o.status = 'paid' after the join: it would remove unpaid orders before total_orders is counted and remove customers without paid orders. Put that condition inside each paid aggregate. CASE with ELSE 0 gives the retained no-order row a zero contribution.

Integer cents avoid floating-point rounding for this small monetary total. The view summarizes orders; it does not charge anyone or infer payment from an amount. Checks include two customers sharing a name, a customer with no orders and unpaid orders that must not count toward revenue. Display the final view ordered by customer_id.
after: Conditional aggregation means choosing which values go into a summary. A CASE inside SUM can count paid orders while another column counts all orders.
Start with customers and LEFT JOIN their orders. Use COUNT(o.id) to count real orders. COUNT(*) would also count the unmatched row kept for a customer with no orders.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE demo_orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, status TEXT, cents INTEGER);
INSERT INTO demo_customers VALUES (1, 'Rin'), (2, 'Sam');
INSERT INTO demo_orders VALUES
  (10, 1, 'paid', 300), (11, 1, 'pending', 500), (12, 1, 'paid', 200);
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN o.cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM demo_customers AS c
LEFT JOIN demo_orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
```
Rin has `3` total orders, `2` paid orders, and `500` paid cents. Sam has `0` for all three.
Group by customer ID and name. Two people can share a name, so grouping by name alone could wrongly combine their orders.
The CASE choices use ELSE 0. A customer with no order contributes zero to each paid total. COUNT(o.id) also gives zero because the unmatched order ID is NULL.
Do not filter the whole joined result to paid orders. That would lose unpaid orders from total_orders and could remove customers with no paid orders.

Create `customer_orders(customer_id, name, total_orders, paid_orders, paid_cents)` from customers and orders. Keep every customer. For paid_cents, use the supplied amount_cents. These small totals use whole cents. Display the view in customer_id order and keep both source tables unchanged.

before: Use `LEFT JOIN` to match customers to orders by customer ID.
Use one `CASE` expression to count paid orders.
Use another `CASE` expression to add paid amounts.
Group the results by customer ID and name.
after: LEFT JOIN orders to customers using the customer ID.
Use CASE inside each paid sum.
Group by ID and name, then create the view.

before: Start from customers so people without orders remain.
Use SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
For paid_cents, use o.amount_cents instead of 1; do not filter the whole query to paid rows.
after: Use 1 for a paid order's count and amount_cents for its paid amount.
Use ELSE 0 for rows that are not paid.
Keep the paid test out of the query's WHERE.

before.question: After a LEFT JOIN, a customer with no orders has one retained row with o.id = NULL. What does COUNT(o.id) return for them?
before.explanation: COUNT(o.id) counts non-NULL IDs, so there are zero orders. COUNT(*) would instead count the retained placeholder row.

after.question: A customer has no orders, so the LEFT JOIN keeps a row with o.id = NULL. What is COUNT(o.id)?
after.explanation: COUNT(o.id) skips NULL IDs, so it counts zero orders.

headings: Return zero when there are no orders

project.title: An order status dashboard
project.task: Create customer_orders with the requested columns. Keep every customer, count all orders, count paid orders, and total only paid amounts in cents.
project.done_when: Customers with no orders have zeros, same-name customers stay separate, paid totals exclude unpaid orders, and source tables stay unchanged.
